item.title: AWS Network Firewall Adds Context-Aware Rules and Next Generation Policies
item.description:
AWS Network Firewall Adds Context-Aware Rules and Next Generation Policies

AWS Network Firewall has updated its capabilities to support context-aware rules, allowing you to match traffic based on the AWS resources that send and receive it rather than by their IP addresses. Alongside this, AWS has introduced Next Generation policies, which separate access control and threat protection into independent engines to help simplify firewall management and policy scaling.

🔍 Overview

Rules that match on IP addresses must keep up with every workload that scales out, is replaced, or moves. Short-lived workloads are the hardest to keep up with; for example, a VPC-attached AWS Lambda function can scale out and start sending traffic before an updated IP list reaches the firewall. Context-aware rules solve this issue by allowing you to filter a function’s traffic by the security group attached to it, or by naming a virtual private cloud (VPC), a subnet, or a transit gateway attachment.

🧩 How it works

Context-aware rules require transit gateway-attached firewalls and function by combining a control path and a data path:

  • The Control Path: A context store—which is a catalog of the AWS resources that can send and receive traffic through a transit gateway—tells the firewall which resources exist. You create this in AWS Network Manager and associate it with the transit gateway that your firewall uses.
  • The Data Path: The transit gateway adds the context of the sender (including its VPC, subnet, transit gateway attachment, and security groups) to each packet.
  • The Firewall Engine: The firewall receives these two paths, reads the context on each packet, and matches it against your configured rules. Source context works with every protocol, while destination context requires TCP-based rules because the firewall learns the receiving resource from return traffic.

Here is how context rules apply to specific AWS resources:

Resource Type Rule Application
Subnet or VPC Applies to each new resource that you launch in it.
Security Group Applies to each new resource whose network interface has that security group attached.
Transit Gateway Attachment Applies to traffic that enters through that attachment.

⚙️ Next Generation Policies

In a Classic policy, your access rules and threat rules run together in a single stateful engine and share one rule capacity. With Next Generation policies, access control and threat protection each get their own stateful engine in the same firewall, executed in sequence:

  1. Firewall Engine: This engine handles access control and is drop by default. Built on Suricata 8 firewall mode, it follows each connection through its entire flow (including the TCP handshake and TLS client hello) and evaluates rules along the way up to the application layer.
  2. IPS Engine: This engine manages threat protection and is pass by default. Traffic allowed by the firewall engine moves here, where the IPS engine checks it using AWS managed rule groups or custom rules that you write.

Because each engine has its own rule capacity, adding access rules does not take capacity away from threat protection. This design allows networking and security teams to work independently on their own configurations without risk of overwriting each other’s rules.

#AWS #NetworkFirewall #CloudSecurity #VPC #TransitGateway

Source: Introducing context-aware rules for AWS Network Firewall | Amazon Web Services Source: Introducing AWS Network Firewall Next Generation policy | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Exposed API Leads to Customer Credential Exposure at Radware
item.description:
Exposed API Leads to Customer Credential Exposure at Radware

Cybersecurity company Radware experienced a data breach after an unauthorized party accessed an unauthenticated internal Cloud WAF management API left reachable from the public internet on November 19, 2026.

🔍 Incident Overview

Radware detected the unauthorized access on a Thursday, ten hours after the initial intrusion. Upon detection, the company took several immediate response actions:

  • Blocked the originating IP address and disabled public access to the internal management API.
  • Revoked and replaced all internal account credentials.
  • Initiated a root cause analysis report, which was later shared by an anonymous source with BleepingComputer.

Founded in 1996 and headquartered in Tel Aviv, Radware provides application delivery and DDoS protection services to more than 12,500 enterprise and telecom carrier customers worldwide.

⚙️ Impacted Systems and Data

The exposure was limited to specific account management details and log export configurations, while core traffic inspection remained unaffected.

System / Data Category Status According to Radware
Customer contact details Potentially accessed
Log export credentials (AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, SFTP) Potentially accessed for a subset of customers
WAF traffic inspection and certificates Not exposed
End-users’ data and customer application traffic Not exposed
Cloud DDoS services and data Not exposed

Radware stated that WAF traffic inspection and protection have continued without interruption, with no evidence found of policy changes or access to customer application traffic.

💡 Customer Action Advised

Radware strongly advised affected AppSec (WAF, BOT) customers to take immediate remedial steps:

  • Rotate exposed Cloud WAF log export credentials, including Azure Blob Storage keys or SAS tokens, AWS S3 access keys, or SFTP credentials, as soon as possible.
  • Review access logs on cloud storage accounts for unexpected access dating back to at least November 19.

The company noted it has already received reports from customers regarding AWS alerts for an unfamiliar IP address attempting to access their log-export buckets.

📊 Investigation and Public Response

Radware is continuing to investigate the incident to determine whether any exposed API keys or customer information were used without authorization. As of the report, Radware has not issued a public statement, filed a breach report with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, or provided an immediate response to inquiries from BleepingComputer.

#Cybersecurity #DataBreach #Radware #CloudSecurity #APISecurity

Source: Radware discloses breach exposing customer cloud access keys

item.title: AWS Enhances API and AI Endpoint Security
item.description:
AWS Enhances API and AI Endpoint Security

AWS has launched new capabilities to discover and protect APIs and AI endpoints, addressing the evolving landscape of digital business and AI agent interactions.

🔍 Overview

  • AWS has introduced new features to help discover and protect APIs and AI endpoints.
  • This includes API Portal in Amazon API Gateway, API Security, and AI Security managed rule groups in AWS WAF.

🧩 How it works

  • API Portal discovers APIs and AI endpoints from configuration and live traffic.
  • API Security protects against broken object level authorization, authentication attacks, and reconnaissance.
  • AI Security identifies AI traffic, validates requests, and checks prompts and responses through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

⚙️ Key details

  • API Portal is available in the Amazon API Gateway console.
  • API Security and AI Security are available in the AWS WAF console.
  • The new features work with Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, and Application Load Balancer.

🚀 Availability

  • API Portal, API Security, and AI Security are generally available today.

💡 Why it matters

  • APIs have run digital businesses for over a decade.
  • In 2026, AI endpoints joined them, leading to a need for new security measures.
  • AI agents now act on behalf of users, requiring robust protection of APIs and AI endpoints.

#AWS #APISecurity #AIEndpoints #CloudSecurity #DigitalBusiness

Source: Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS extends Trusted Identity Propagation to IAM Federation and Roles Anywhere
item.description:
AWS extends Trusted Identity Propagation to IAM Federation and Roles Anywhere

AWS has extended Trusted Identity Propagation (TIP) to support IAM federation and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, enabling customers to grant access and audit activity based on the specific user or workload behind an IAM role.

🔍 Overview

Trusted Identity Propagation (TIP) carries the identity of a user or workload with each AWS request. This allows users to grant permissions to that specific user or workload and trace its actions in AWS CloudTrail. Previously, TIP was available only for users accessing AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center. The new extension makes TIP work for users and workloads that federate directly into IAM roles or use X.509 certificates to obtain AWS credentials, while also simplifying TIP usage with IAM Identity Center.

🧩 How it works

TIP addresses the gap where access control decisions apply to the role rather than the user, and CloudTrail attributes each action to the role session. By attaching identity context from a trusted source to the role session at credential issuance, TIP provides a stable reference for the user or workload behind each request. This context is immutable for the lifetime of the session and can include optional claims, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name.

The identity context propagates through supported downstream requests:

  • Role Assumption: When a TIP session assumes another role, AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) carries the context into the new role session.
  • Forward Access Sessions (FAS): When an AWS service makes a downstream request on your behalf, FAS credentials carry the identity context.
  • Outbound Federation: With IAM outbound identity federation, the session can request a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries identity context to an external service.

⚙️ Key details

AWS validates the source and attaches identity context through three primary paths:

Path Source of Identity Context Trusted Source Type
IAM Federation SAML assertion or OIDC token External SAML or OIDC Identity Providers (IdP)
IAM Identity Center Username received from identity source IAM Identity Center
IAM Roles Anywhere X.509 certificate X.509 certificates

TIP context propagates to a new role session only under specific boundary conditions:

  • The target role is in the account where the identity provider is configured.
  • The target role is in another account within the same AWS organization.

IAM policies evaluate this identity context to authorize requests, and AWS CloudTrail records it for auditing. For example, Amazon S3 bucket policies and AWS Lambda can utilize this context for access control and audit logging. The identity context is represented through context keys, including the aws:OriginIdentity/* namespace, which serves as the common namespace for identity information across all three paths.

#AWS #IAM #CloudSecurity #IdentityManagement #CloudTrail #DevSecOps

Source: Know the identity behind the role: Authorize and audit with trusted identity propagation | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Simplifies WAF Pricing with Three-Dimensional Model
item.description:
AWS Simplifies WAF Pricing with Three-Dimensional Model

📊 Overview

Starting today, AWS WAF pricing is easier to predict. Your bill is now based on three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply to that traffic. For new or smaller workloads, the Free plan of CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans is another way to start. If your application serves fewer than 1 million requests per month, the Free plan costs $0 per month for each CloudFront distribution. It includes AWS WAF protection against common web threats, DDoS protection, and the CloudFront CDN, with no overage charges.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Adding a protection (such as a rule, Bot Control, or Anti-DDoS rule group) no longer adds a subscription or a separate per-request charge. Those requests bill at the base request rate.
  • Capacity no longer affects your rate. Each protection pack (web ACL) now includes up to 2,500 web ACL capacity units (WCUs), up from 1,500, and going past your included capacity does not raise what you pay per request.
  • The premium request fee applies only to the traffic you choose to send through advanced protections.
  • You can estimate costs before writing a first rule, and those estimates hold even as your rules change.
  • Security rules change often. Adding, reordering, or removing rules does not change your rate.
  • For AWS Shield Advanced subscribers, nothing changes. Your Shield Advanced subscription, its price, and your included AWS WAF entitlement stay the same.
  • Customers on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan also see no change.

💰 How Costs Are Calculated

AWS WAF bills three fees:

Fee Type Description
Resource Fee Hourly charge for each resource associated with a protection pack (e.g., CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, Amazon API Gateway APIs).
Base Request Fee Applies to each request AWS WAF inspects.
Premium Request Fee Applies on top of the base request fee, to requests evaluated by advanced protections like Bot Control, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security.

Both API Security and AI Security use the same premium request fee, with no separate subscription or rate. Requests evaluated by one or more advanced protections are billed $5.60 per million: the $0.60 base request fee plus the $5.00 premium request fee. AWS WAF charges the premium request fee once per request, however many advanced protections evaluate it. A request blocked before reaching an advanced protection pays only the base request fee.

🚀 Availability and Transition

  • Existing AWS WAF customers move to the new pricing on February 1, 2027. Until then, they keep their current pricing and don’t need to do anything at launch.
  • If you hold an AWS WAF private pricing agreement, it stays in force until it expires.
  • The new pricing includes the Security analytics dashboard, which shows full traffic metrics for your protected applications over a rolling 21-day window at no additional cost.

💡 Example: Cost Estimation

Here’s a worked example from the AWS WAF pricing page:

Example 1: One protected resource (Application Load Balancer) serving 20 million requests per month.

  • Resource fee: 1 resource × $0.01 per hour × 730 hours = $7.30
  • Base request fee: 20 million × $0.60 per million = $12.00
  • Total: $19.30 per month

For more pricing details and examples, visit the AWS WAF pricing page. If you have questions about how the new pricing applies to your account, contact your AWS account team or open a Support case.

#AWS #WAF #CloudSecurity #Pricing

Source: Introducing AWS WAF simplified pricing | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Shared Responsibility for AI Agents Remains Undefined Across Major Vendors
item.description:
Shared Responsibility for AI Agents Remains Undefined Across Major Vendors

Five organizations have published guidance on responsibility for AI agents, but no consensus has emerged on who is ultimately responsible for agent behavior. While traditional cloud security has clear separation of duties between vendors and customers, AI agents act as non-deterministic intermediaries, making the separation of responsibilities less clean. The available guidance approaches the issue from different angles, ranging from specific task assignments to descriptions of broader security layers. To address this, organizations need to determine who owns each agent, what permissions it holds, and how it operates across systems.

🧩 How it works

In cloud security, models like the AWS Shared Responsibility Model establish a clear division: vendors handle infrastructure security, while customers are responsible for the data and the actions taken. For example, if data is copied from AWS to SFDC, each vendor secures their infrastructure, but the customer owns the action.

AI agents complicate this framework. They send authenticated, authorized requests that can be compromised or rogue. A rogue agent has either misunderstood its instructions or acted inappropriately—a type of error that is not necessarily a mistake in the human sense. Because agents act as intermediaries between the user and the request, and they are not deterministic by nature, the line between vendor and customer responsibility becomes blurred.

⚙️ Key details

Five specific organizations have published guidance on this topic:

  • Microsoft: Published an AI agent shared responsibility model featuring a matrix for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS deployments.
  • CSA and CoSAI: Published shared responsibility models.
  • AWS: Provided security guidance for AgentCore, applying its general shared responsibility model without a specific agent-specific model.
  • Anthropic: Published guidance titled “Trustworthy agents in practice.”

Only two of these organizations assign ownership of an agent’s identity, and they split that ownership differently. No publication agrees on who is responsible for the agent’s behavior. Approaches vary: some assign specific tasks to providers and customers, while others describe security layers or broader stakeholder roles.

💡 Why it matters

Frontier AI labs are clear about their immediate responsibilities: making models more robust, better guarded, and harder to hijack. They are equally clear about their limitations: they cannot understand the specific business context of an action. For instance, an agent deleting files from Google Drive could be acting maliciously or performing a normal task; the system cannot distinguish between the two. Consequently, builders bear final responsibility for the behavior and permissions of the systems they assemble. While tools like Claude Code include checks such as automated classifiers to block actions driven by hostile content, and vendors like OpenAI, Cursor, and GitHub offer approval prompts and sandboxes, these capabilities do not automatically resolve the question of accountability. As new protocols like MCP are introduced, they may conceptually denote expanded responsibility for those who built them, but the lack of unified ownership remains a critical gap for organizations deploying agents.

#AIAgents #CloudSecurity #Microsoft #AWS #Anthropic #SharedResponsibility

Source: AI Agents Are Creating a Shared Responsibility Gap

item.title: Rackspace Spot Breach Exposes Kubernetes Secrets and API Tokens
item.description:
Rackspace Spot Breach Exposes Kubernetes Secrets and API Tokens

Rackspace has warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials. The intrusion allowed unauthorized parties to deploy workloads and access sensitive Kubernetes secrets within customer clusters.

🔍 Overview

Rackspace disclosed the breach in a notification to affected customers, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November 17, 2026, between approximately 00:20 and 22:00 UTC. The company learned of the intrusion on November 18 after receiving a customer report and confirmed that the recipient’s organization was affected that same day.

⚙️ Key details

  • Access Method: An unauthorized party used leaked credentials to act as legitimate users in some customer organizations.
  • Actions Taken: Attackers created pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and volumes.
  • Exposure Risk: Attackers could have read any Secret stored in an affected user’s clusters, as well as any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens held by that user.
  • Indicators: The breach was associated with IP address 23.224.79.106, IP range 23.224.0.0/15, and suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes including i1, glm-, and probe.

🛡️ Remediation and Response

Rackspace stated that it has revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and strengthened access controls and monitoring. Affected customers were instructed to:

  • Reissue their Spot API tokens.
  • Replace refresh tokens used in automation tools.
  • Download fresh Kubernetes configuration files.
  • Rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets.
  • Analyze logs associated with databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services dating back to November 17 to identify possible abuse of exposed credentials.

The breach caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console, temporarily preventing customers from managing their clusters or rotating credentials. Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and Chief Growth Officer of Platform9, explained that the team deliberately disabled access while securing its infrastructure. Rackspace announced that service was fully restored on November 21.

#Rackspace #Kubernetes #CloudSecurity #DataBreach

Source: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets

item.title: AWS Introduces GetScopedCredentials API to Safely Scope Down Temporary Security Credentials
item.description:
AWS Introduces GetScopedCredentials API to Safely Scope Down Temporary Security Credentials

AWS has launched GetScopedCredentials, a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that enables you to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security credentials. This feature is designed to help secure workloads, such as AI agents, by ensuring they only have the minimum permissions needed to perform their tasks rather than the full permissions of the calling session.

🔍 Overview

GetScopedCredentials provides a programmatic way to generate narrower security credentials from those you already possess. You can assign each agent, sub-agent, or process its own credentials that carry reduced permissions, a shorter session duration, or both, while keeping the original caller’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity.

Because GetScopedCredentials works by narrowing the credentials you already have, it acts as a building block that you can integrate directly into:

  • Agent frameworks
  • Continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines
  • Services that issue credentials to other components
  • Custom applications

🧩 How it works

To call the API, you must have valid temporary security credentials and the necessary permissions to call GetScopedCredentials. You can make the call using the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language.

The technical specifications of the API include:

  • Input Credentials: You can call the API with the temporary credentials you already use, including those from aws login, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance profile, or an AWS Lambda function.
  • Scope Down Policy: In each call, you pass a scope down policy (an inline policy representing the maximum permissions) of up to 2,048 characters.
  • Intersection of Permissions: The resulting permissions are the intersection of the session’s effective permissions and the scope down policy. This ensures that permissions can only be reduced, never expanded.
  • Session Duration: You can request a shorter session duration, which cannot exceed the remaining duration of the calling session.
  • Chaining Calls: You can call GetScopedCredentials again using the resulting scoped-down credentials to restrict permissions or reduce duration even further. This allows an orchestrating agent to give sub-agents narrower access than its own.

💡 Common Use Cases

GetScopedCredentials can be applied whenever a workload requires narrower access than the session that initiates it. Notable use cases include:

  • Limiting AI Agent Actions: AI agents decide on actions at runtime based on prompts or tool output. By using GetScopedCredentials, you can restrict their actions to only what is required—such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket—or explicitly strip away risky actions like deleting resources. Run your agents in sandbox environments, such as AWS Strands Box, to ensure they only access these restricted credentials.
  • Scoping Down Based on Runtime Context: Some workloads run under a single IAM role but require different permissions based on authenticated requests. For example, a multi-tenant application with a single IAM role that serves files from different prefixes in one S3 bucket can use a trusted credential broker to call GetScopedCredentials. The broker obtains credentials restricted to only the specific tenant’s prefix and passes them to the worker.
  • Just-in-Time Access: Securing tasks based on runtime data learned only after the workload begins.

#AWS #Security #IAM #AIAgents #CloudSecurity

Source: Scope down permissions of existing sessions using AWS STS GetScopedCredentials | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS re:Invent 2026 to Showcase AWS Continuum and Security for AI Agents
item.description:
AWS re:Invent 2026 to Showcase AWS Continuum and Security for AI Agents

The AWS Security, Identity, and Governance team has announced the security session lineup for AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas, running from November 30 to December 4, 2026. The event will showcase new developments in AWS Continuum, a service designed to automate security workflows, alongside sessions on governance and authentication for autonomous AI agents.

🔍 Overview

AWS re:Invent 2026 features nearly 120 security sessions across breakouts, chalk talks, workshops, code talks, builders’ sessions, and lightning talks. Security sessions begin Monday morning and run through Friday, with Tuesday and Wednesday sessions distributed across the Wynn, MGM Grand, and Caesars Palace. On Thursday, December 3, the Wynn venue hosts a full day of advanced security sessions with 78 sessions from 8:00 AM to 5:30 PM, the majority of which are at the 300 level or above. This includes 12 workshops, 11 builders’ sessions, and 22 chalk talks.

⚙️ Key Sessions for AWS Continuum and Security

The event includes dedicated sessions detailing the capabilities of AWS Continuum and secure architectures for AI workloads:

Session Day & Time Format Description
SEC388 Monday 10:00 AM Breakout National Institutes of Health shares how it manages identity lifecycle across clouds.
SEC302 Monday 10:00 AM Breakout Building a governance foundation for AI workloads that grows with autonomous agents.
SEC427 Monday 12:00 PM Code Talk Threat models an agentic development workflow from user story to deployment with AWS Continuum.
SEC424 Tuesday 2:30 PM Chalk Talk How IAM evaluates policies on every request.
SEC312 Tuesday 3:30 PM Workshop Run an on-demand penetration test against a live application with AWS Continuum.
SEC323 Tuesday 3:30 PM Workshop Recover from a simulated ransomware event and prove the restore is clean.
SEC362 Thursday 8:00 AM Workshop Build authentication, authorization, and audit for AI agents.
SEC349 Thursday 8:30 AM Workshop Build a layered controls stack for a fleet of agents.
SEC419 Thursday 11:30 AM Chalk Talk OAuth delegation patterns for agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.
SEC405 Thursday 12:00 PM Builders’ Session Take a vulnerable application from discovery to fix with Amazon Inspector, AWS Continuum, and Amazon GuardDuty.
SEC501 Thursday 1:00 PM Breakout Goes inside the research behind the GuardDuty detection engine.
SEC311 Thursday 1:00 PM Builders’ Session Wires AWS frontier agents into an automated find-and-fix security loop.
SEC384 Thursday 2:30 PM Breakout How AWS Continuum discovers, validates, and fixes code vulnerabilities in one workflow.
SEC390 Thursday 4:00 PM Breakout Woodside handed SOC monitoring to AWS Security Incident Response to focus on threat hunting.

🎤 Keynotes and Featured Speakers

Several key leadership presentations are scheduled for the event:

  • Chet Kapoor (AWS VP of Security, Search, and Observability) presents “The Future of Security” at 11:00 AM.
  • Amy Herzog (AWS Chief Information Security Officer) presents “The Old Security Playbook Is Dead” at 1:00 PM.
  • Eric Brandwine (VP/Distinguished Engineer, AWS Security) presents “Operationalizing security for the future with best practices today” at 3:00 PM.

The Thursday keynote runs from 8:30 to 10:00 AM at The Venetian and is also streamed online.

#AWS #reInvent #CloudSecurity #AWSContinuum #AIAgents

Source: Your AWS Security, Identity, and Governance guide to re:Invent 2026 | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS WAF Introduces New Security Analytics Dashboard
item.description:
AWS WAF Introduces New Security Analytics Dashboard

AWS has introduced a new security analytics dashboard for AWS WAF, providing a single global page to investigate traffic across all protection packs (web ACLs), Regional resources, and Amazon CloudFront distributions. This update builds on the 2024 traffic overview dashboard by offering a consolidated view that helps users act on findings faster.

🔍 Overview

The new dashboard is designed to help users investigate and contain threats faster while reducing false positives that block real customers. Key aspects of the update include:

  • A single global page for investigating traffic across all protection packs (web ACLs).
  • Coverage of Regional resources and Amazon CloudFront distributions.
  • No need to build or maintain a custom log analytics pipeline.
  • Built on full-fidelity request data rather than samples.
  • Two primary use cases demonstrated: investigating a traffic spike and tuning rules to reduce false positives.

🧩 How It Works

To access the dashboard, users navigate to the AWS WAF console and select “Security analytics” in the navigation pane. The interface allows users to narrow the view to specific protection packs and set time ranges.

  • Global View: The dashboard displays request data across all protection packs in the account. Selecting “All protection packs” shows a comprehensive view.
  • Traffic Breakdown: The top of the page shows total requests split by action: Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, and Challenge.
  • Charts and Widgets: The “Requests chart” visualizes traffic changes over time, while widgets below display top values for specific dimensions. Users can split the Requests chart by dimensions such as Host, Rule triggered, Country, or JA4.
  • Host Grouping: Grouping or filtering by Host identifies which domains are under attack or experiencing spikes, even when a single protection pack protects multiple domains or a domain spans several protection packs.
  • Labels and Detections: AWS Managed Rules add labels (e.g., Bot Control categories, verification status, and signals like non_browser_user_agent). Users can also create custom labels. Because labels are recorded even when a rule is set to count-only, filtering by a label shows what a rule detected across all protection packs without changing how traffic is handled.
  • Filters and Actions: Filters apply to the entire dashboard, updating the action split, Requests chart, widgets, and request list. Users can select any value in a widget to focus on it, remove it, or block it.
  • Request Details: For individual requests, the dashboard displays HTTP fields such as host, path, headers, user agent, and JA4 fingerprint. It also shows which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted.

⚙️ Key Details

Previously, accessing this level of detail required working from a limited sample of requests or setting up and querying custom AWS WAF logs. The new dashboard makes this data available directly. Additionally, the current dashboard view is saved in the user’s browser.

💡 Why It Matters

This tool allows security teams to move from reactive log analysis to proactive investigation and containment. By providing full-fidelity data without the overhead of maintaining custom pipelines, organizations can more effectively tune their rules to minimize false positives and protect their infrastructure.

#AWS #WAF #WebSecurity #CloudSecurity #DataAnalytics

Source: Introducing the new AWS WAF security analytics dashboard | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Databricks Mitigates and Patches Java4Shell OpenJDK Vulnerability
item.description:
Databricks Mitigates and Patches Java4Shell OpenJDK Vulnerability

Databricks has addressed the industry-wide OpenJDK vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) before its public disclosure. The company is protecting its platform and customers through a two-phase response: immediate mitigation and subsequent patching.

🔍 Overview

Prior to Java4Shell’s public disclosure, Databricks was already addressing the vulnerability. The company is protecting customers in two phases: quick mitigation to disable use of the vulnerable code, and then patching to replace the vulnerable code.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Databricks has applied the mitigation to its platform, disabling use of vulnerable code for all supported versions of Databricks Runtime.
  • The mitigation is not expected to have a meaningful performance impact on customers.
  • To apply the mitigation as quickly as possible, Databricks took the rare step of proactively restarting affected clusters.
  • While the mitigation blocks the attack, in an abundance of caution, Databricks will provide patched versions of supported Databricks Runtimes.
  • Databricks has no evidence to indicate any unauthorized access to its products, services, or customers’ data.

🚀 Availability

Customer Type Patch Delivery Method
Serverless platform customers Patches will be applied automatically
Classic cluster customers Customers need to restart their clusters
Customers running custom images Databricks is reaching out to them

💡 Why It Matters

Databricks has stated it has no evidence to indicate any unauthorized access to Databricks products, services, or customers’ data. The proactive mitigation and planned patching demonstrate the company’s response to the vulnerability.

#Databricks #Java4Shell #OpenJDK #Security #Vulnerability #CloudSecurity

Source: Java4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2026-114938) assessment

item.title: F5 Patches NGINX nginx2root Vulnerabilities Enabling Remote Code Execution
item.description:
F5 Patches NGINX nginx2root Vulnerabilities Enabling Remote Code Execution

F5 has released security updates for multiple NGINX vulnerabilities, including two critical flaws dubbed “nginx2root.” These vulnerabilities allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable web servers and can be chained with a Linux kernel bug to gain root access to the underlying host.

Researchers at Xint, Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, and Rapid7 discovered the two primary HTTP/2 vulnerabilities independently. Xint researchers demonstrated that by chaining one of these flaws with a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s SCTP subsystem, an attacker can escape an NGINX Docker container and gain root privileges.

🧩 How it works

The “nginx2root” vulnerabilities involve memory corruption and session management errors within the NGINX worker process:

  • CVE-2026-123007: A flow-control bug that causes memory corruption in an NGINX worker. It impacts versions 1.31.8 down to 1.9.5.
  • CVE-2026-123633: A use-after-free issue that occurs when NGINX accepts HTTP/2 connections and proxies them to a backend. When the worker runs low on connection slots, it may close an active connection and free memory that a request is still using.

⚙️ Key details

Vulnerability Description
CVE-2026-123007 Memory corruption flaw in NGINX worker via HTTP/2 flow-control.
CVE-2026-123633 Use-after-free vulnerability affecting HTTP/2 requests proxied to backends.
CVE-2026-118899 High-severity DoS flaw causing an infinite loop over TLS 1.3.
CVE-2026-121810 Use-after-free vulnerability affecting HTTP/3 reverse proxying.
CVE-2026-123634 Use-after-free vulnerability affecting DNS resolution with subrequests.
CVE-2026-113425 Use-after-free vulnerability affecting mail proxy authentication.

🚀 Availability

F5 has fixed these issues in the latest versions of NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus. System administrators are recommended to upgrade immediately:

  • NGINX Open Source: Update to 1.30.7 (stable) or 1.31.9 (mainline).
  • NGINX Plus: Update to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1.

As a temporary mitigation for the two “nginx2root” flaws, administrators can disable HTTP/2, although this does not address the other vulnerabilities included in the security update.

💡 Why it matters

Exploitability depends heavily on specific server configurations. Security researcher Florian Roth notes that these flaws are exploitable in non-default configurations and may not be an imminent threat for most deployments. The vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on a reachable listener, and CVE-2026-123633 specifically requires NGINX to be proxying requests to a backend.

According to Censys, approximately 8.8 million NGINX services were potentially exposed to CVE-2026-123007 as of November 19, based on version numbers and HTTP/2 support. More than 511,000 previously exposed services have already been patched or mitigated.

#Cybersecurity #NGINX #InfoSec #Linux #CloudSecurity

Source: Critical NGINX ‘NGINX2Root’ bugs let attackers hijack servers

item.title: AWS Agent Registry Introduces Custom Metadata Schemas for Structured Governance
item.description:
AWS Agent Registry Introduces Custom Metadata Schemas for Structured Governance

Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. This update allows administrators to define a set of organization-specific key-value pairs that registry records must carry, enabling structured validation, discovery, and governance.

🔍 Overview

AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog to register, approve, and discover resources and custom records. Each record within the registry carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. With the introduction of custom metadata schemas, administrators can enforce structured metadata on every record to maintain consistency across teams.

⚙️ How it works

A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs. The registry administrator defines the schema—including field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional—and applies it to the registry.

Key behaviors of the schema validation include:

  • Supported Field Types: Each field can be configured as Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean.
  • Scope of Fields: The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and administrators can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types.
  • Enforcement and Validation: When a record is created or updated, AWS Agent Registry validates the custom metadata against the schema. If a record includes an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, it is rejected with a ValidationException.
  • Compliance Status: If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT. Calling GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status.

🧩 Supported Fields and Enrichment

Organizations can use custom metadata fields to track ownership, environments, and compliance. Examples of these fields include:

  • Environment & Ownership: Fields such as environment (prod, staging, or dev), businessUnit, ownerTeam, supportContact, and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it.
  • Inventory Integration: A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to an existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for dependents.
  • Security & Compliance: Fields such as data classification, compliance scope (like PCI or HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn approvals into reviews of structured evidence. Existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools can write these values through the API before a record is submitted.

🔍 Discovery and Filtering

Custom metadata values are indexed for search. Approvers can use the validated values when reviewing records, and consumers and agents can use Discovery APIs to filter records based on custom attributes.

For example, a consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as:

1

environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED

To ensure security, only approved records are returned; a record that matches the filters but has not been approved is omitted from the results.

As a use case, AnyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp (a read-only server for ledger lookups). Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function determines whether consumers can discover it.

🚀 Prerequisites

To get started with custom metadata schemas, you need:

  • An AWS account in a supported AWS Region.
  • Python 3.11 or later.
  • boto3 1.43.113 or later.

#AWSAgentRegistry #CloudGovernance #MetadataSchemas #CloudSecurity

Source: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Argus AI Security Platform Launches with Self-Hosted Multi-Tenant Capabilities
item.description:
Argus AI Security Platform Launches with Self-Hosted Multi-Tenant Capabilities

A new self-hosted, multi-tenant, and MIT-licensed security platform named Argus has been released to watch cloud, identity, code, endpoints, network, and Kubernetes environments.

🔍 Overview

Argus catches attacks at machine speed, investigates them with AI agents, and contains them in seconds. The platform operates offline for air-gapped installs and ensures security data never leaves the user’s hands.

🧩 How it works

  • Nine specialist agents triage, investigate, and hunt using read-only tools.
  • Agents can propose a fix but never execute one; their one write-capable tool creates a pending request.
  • Everything agents read is treated as untrusted data so prompt injections become signals instead of hijacks.
  • Autonomous response playbooks act the moment a detection fires using a catalog of 27 typed actions.
  • Every autonomous feature ships off by default so users can enable autonomy gradually.

⚙️ Key details

  • AI Gateway: Puts OpenAI and Anthropic traffic behind org-held keys, model allowlists, data-loss prevention, prompt-injection flags, and budgets.
  • Shadow-AI Discovery: Finds services used without approval via network, cloud, and SSO telemetry.
  • Canaries: Built for agents with hidden prompt injections, agent rules files, a fake MCP server, and fake LLM API keys.
  • Attack Simulator: Replays eight AI-driven attack scenarios in an isolated sandbox tenant.
  • Pentesting: Autopilot and native autonomous pentesting plan tests and run them through a scope-checked harness.
  • Vulnerability Enrichment: CVE findings are enriched with CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list and EPSS scores, automatically raising severity.

🚀 Availability

  • Deployment options include Docker Compose for pilots, Helm for Kubernetes, and Terraform for AWS and Azure.
  • Encrypted backups run on a schedule and land on disk, S3, or Azure with single-command restore and verification checks.
  • Control mappings for SOC 2, NIST 800-171, and ISO 27001 are included.

item.title: Orca Security Deploys Discovery AI on AWS Bedrock to Simplify Cloud Queries
item.description:
Orca Security Deploys Discovery AI on AWS Bedrock to Simplify Cloud Queries

Orca Security has released an update to its Discovery AI service, a natural‑language query agent built on Amazon Bedrock that translates plain‑English questions into Sonar queries for its cloud‑security data graph.

🔍 Overview

  • Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain‑specific query languages.
  • Orca Security’s Sonar system tracks more than 900 cloud resource models (e.g., Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon S3 buckets) and requires JSON queries that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent‑child hierarchies.
  • The original proof‑of‑concept loaded the full Sonar schema (over 900 model definitions) into a single prompt, yielding strong output but high token consumption (~2 million input tokens per workload), high latency (~60 seconds), and limited accuracy on complex multi‑model queries.
  • To address these issues, Orca partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a hybrid Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) solution on Amazon Bedrock that converts natural language into validated Discovery filters.

🧩 How It Works

Discovery AI follows a nine‑step pipeline, matching each stage to the most suitable Bedrock model:

  1. Request Entry and Context Setup – Combines the user’s question with organization, connected cloud providers, and request metadata.
  2. Quick Deterministic Matcher – Uses regex and rule‑based matching to detect high‑confidence patterns such as IP addresses, CVEs, ARNs, file hashes, AMI IDs, Oracle Cloud identifiers, EC2 IDs, URLs, and alert IDs.
  3. Fast‑Path Return – When a deterministic match is found, a predefined Discovery filter is returned without invoking an LLM.
  4. (Subsequent stages) – For unmatched requests, the pipeline proceeds through retrieval, schema‑aware construction, and LLM inference stages to produce a Sonar‑compatible JSON query.

Key design choices:

  • Amazon Bedrock provides access to multiple foundation models through a single API, allowing the team to allocate different models to each pipeline stage without separate integrations.
  • Bedrock inherits AWS governance controls (IAM, VPC endpoints, CloudTrail), satisfying Orca’s security requirements.
  • The model‑agnostic architecture enables swapping newer model versions without re‑architecting the pipeline.

⚙️ Key Results

  • Query costs reduced by 90 % compared with the baseline.
  • Input token usage reduced by 93 %.
  • End‑to‑end latency reduced by 75 %, achieving ~15‑second response times (down from ~60 seconds).
  • The system now handles thousands of queries per day.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Analysts can obtain answers without knowing Sonar’s exact schema or the 18‑operator query language.
  • Lower costs and faster responses make continuous cloud‑security monitoring more practical.
  • The hybrid RAG approach demonstrates how Retrieval‑Augmented Generation can be combined with domain‑specific schemas to improve accuracy on complex multi‑model queries.

#OrcaSecurity #AmazonBedrock #DiscoveryAI #CloudSecurity

Source: Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Bridgecrew launches Checkov for IaC and Open‑Source Package Security Scanning
item.description:
Bridgecrew launches Checkov for IaC and Open‑Source Package Security Scanning

Bridgecrew introduced Checkov, a static code analysis tool for infrastructure‑as‑code (IaC) that also performs software composition analysis (SCA) on container images and open‑source packages, helping developers prevent cloud misconfigurations and discover vulnerabilities early in the build process.

🔍 Overview

  • Checkov scans cloud infrastructure provisioned with Terraform, Terraform plan, CloudFormation, AWS SAM, Kubernetes, Helm charts, Kustomize, Dockerfile, Serverless, Bicep, OpenAPI, ARM Templates, or OpenTofu.
  • It also scans open‑source packages and images for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs).
  • The tool powers Prisma Cloud Application Security, the developer‑first platform that codifies and streamlines cloud security throughout the development lifecycle.

🧩 How it works

  • Uses graph‑based scanning to provide context‑awareness policies.
  • Supports Python format for attribute policies and YAML format for both attribute and composite policies.
  • Detects AWS credentials in EC2 Userdata, Lambda environment variables, and Terraform providers.
  • Identifies secrets using regular expressions, keywords, and entropy‑based detection.

⚙️ Supported platforms

Category Supported Types
IaC templates Terraform, Terraform plan, Terraform JSON, CloudFormation, AWS SAM, Kubernetes, Helm, Kustomize, Dockerfile, Serverless framework, Ansible, Bicep, ARM, OpenTofu
CI pipelines Argo Workflows, Azure Pipelines, BitBucket Pipelines, Circle CI Pipelines, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI workflow files

📋 Key Features

  • Over 1 000 built‑in policies covering security and compliance best practices for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
  • Scans both IaC files and CI workflow definitions.
  • Performs Software Composition Analysis (SCA) for images and open‑source packages.
  • Provides context‑aware, graph‑based detection.
  • Enables policy authoring in Python and YAML.

🔐 Detection capabilities

  • Finds misconfigurations in IaC and cloud resources.
  • Detects AWS credentials in various locations.
  • Identifies secrets using regex, keywords, and entropy detection.
  • Scans container images and open‑source packages for CVEs.

🚀 Availability

  • Checkov is integrated into Prisma Cloud Application Security, delivering continuous security for cloud resources and IaC throughout the development lifecycle.

#Checkov #IaC #SCA #CloudSecurity

item.title: Google introduces private server-side memory to Private AI Compute platform
item.description:
Google introduces private server-side memory to Private AI Compute platform

Google is bringing private, server-side memory to its Private AI Compute platform, enabling the system to securely retain context over time and across devices.

🔍 Overview

Previously, the Private AI Compute platform and similar industry solutions were “stateless,” meaning all context was wiped once a task ended. The new technical capability introduces a persistent memory layer that functions as a secure digital vault in the cloud.

🧩 How it works

  • Storage: Information is sealed within dedicated, encrypted storage.
  • Access Control: Cryptographic keys required to unlock the data are held exclusively on personal devices, making data inaccessible to others, including Google.
  • Connectivity: An authenticated, end-to-end encrypted channel connects the device to a protected, isolated cloud environment known as a “secure enclave.”
  • Processing: The secure enclave temporarily decrypts data in isolated memory to handle requests, saves new context, and immediately encrypts it again.

⚙️ Key details

To support this development, Google has provided the following:

  • An updated technical whitepaper.
  • A tamper-proof public record of server software, allowing devices to verify the software is authentic and unaltered before sending personal data.
  • An update on technical methods, including results from an independent audit by a leading cybersecurity firm.

This research was co-developed by Google DeepMind, Platforms & Devices, Core and Cloud teams, with executive sponsorship from Four Flynn, Jay Yagnik, and David Kleidermacher.

#PrivateAICompute #CloudSecurity #GoogleDeepMind #Encryption #Privacy

Source: Advancing confidential AI with secure memory
